outputs.final_proof:
\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space. We prove that for every $x\in X$ and every open set $U$ containing $x$, there is an open set $V$ containing $x$ such that $\overline{V}\subseteq U$.

Choose an open neighborhood $W$ of $x$ with compact closure $K=\overline{W}$. Replace $W$ by $W\cap U$, so that $W\subseteq U$ and $K$ remains compact after taking the closure of the new $W$; denote this closure again by $K$. Let $C=K\setminus U$. This is compact and does not contain $x$. For each $y\in C$, choose disjoint open sets $N_y$ containing $x$ and $M_y$ containing $y$. Finitely many $M_{y_1},\ldots,M_{y_n}$ cover $C$. Define
\[
V=W\cap N_{y_1}\cap\cdots\cap N_{y_n}.
\]
Then $V$ is open and contains $x$. Since $V\subseteq W\subseteq U$, we have $\overline V\subseteq\overline W=K$. If $z\in\overline V\cap C$, then $z\in M_{y_i}$ for some $i$, but $V\subseteq N_{y_i}$ and $N_{y_i}\cap M_{y_i}=\varnothing$, contradicting $z\in\overline V$. Hence $\overline V\cap C=\varnothing$, so $\overline V\subseteq U$.

Now let $F$ be closed and $x\notin F$. Apply the property to $U=X\setminus F$ to obtain $V$ with $x\in V$ and $\overline V\subseteq X\setminus F$. Thus $V$ and $X\setminus\overline V$ are disjoint open neighborhoods of $x$ and $F$. Together with the $T_1$ property supplied by Hausdorffness, this proves that $X$ is regular.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space. We verify the point--closed-set definition of regularity. Hausdorffness implies the $T_1$ axiom.

Let $F$ be closed in $X$ and let $x\in X\setminus F$. Set $U=X\setminus F$. By local compactness, choose an open neighborhood $W$ of $x$ such that $K=\overline W$ is compact. Replace $W$ by $W\cap U$; then $W\subseteq U$ and, after replacing $K$ by the closure of this new $W$, $K$ is still compact. Let $C=K\cap F$. This is a compact subset of the Hausdorff space $X$.

For each $y\in C$, choose disjoint open neighborhoods $N_y$ of $x$ and $M_y$ of $y$. By compactness, finitely many $M_{y_1},\ldots,M_{y_n}$ cover $C$. Put
\[
V=W\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^n N_{y_i}.
\]
Then $V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ and $\overline V\subseteq K$. If $z\in\overline V\cap F$, then $z\in K\cap F=C$, so $z\in M_{y_i}$ for some $i$. But $V\subseteq N_{y_i}$ and $N_{y_i}\cap M_{y_i}=\varnothing$, whereas $z\in\overline V$ and $M_{y_i}$ is an open neighborhood of $z$, which is impossible. Therefore $\overline V\cap F=\varnothing$.

Consequently, $V$ and $X\setminus\overline V$ are disjoint open neighborhoods of $x$ and $F$. Hence $X$ is regular.
\end{proof}
